label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
I’ve read these monthly threads for a long time but never posted. I’m posting tonight because something happened at work today and I’m still carrying it around with me. I’ll keep the details vague for privacy, but I wanted to write about Mrs. H.

Mrs. H. had been one of my weekly blister pack patients for years. She lived on her own after her husband died and came in with her cane, week after week. Somehow, a medication pickup was never just a medication pickup with her.

Most weeks she brought me something. Often it was poppy seed cake. Once it was a jar of pickles that I honestly had no idea what to do with, but I took home anyway because she was so pleased to give it to me. During Ramadan, she remembered that I was fasting. She wrapped my piece of cake in foil, wrote my name on it, and told me very seriously that I was not allowed to eat it before sunset.

A few years ago, after a new doctor added a medication, I caught a potentially serious interaction and called to get it sorted out. She told everybody that I had saved her life. I kept telling her I had only done my job. That was true. I still think it was just my job. But she never stopped bringing it up.

She passed away recently. Today her daughter came in to return the unused packs and her glucometer. I knew this visit would probably happen one day, but knowing that doesn’t prepare you for standing there taking back medications with your patient’s name on them and days still left in the pack.

Her daughter also gave me a card. Her mother had written it some time ago but never gave it to me. In her handwriting, she called me her “Arabic daughter.”

That was the end of my composure. My tech saw my face and covered the counter for ten minutes while I went into the back room and cried. Then I came back out and carried on with the afternoon, because there were still prescriptions to check and people waiting. It felt strange how ordinary the rest of the day had to be.

My father was a pharmacist in Egypt. He knew all the families who came to him, not just their prescriptions. When I came to Canada, I thought community pharmacy here would be different. In some ways it is, of course, but in that way it isn’t at all. People become part of your week. Then, without you really noticing when it happened, they become part of your life.

School taught us pharmacology, interactions, dosing, how to make the call to a prescriber. Nobody taught us how to say goodbye to a patient, or what to do when their daughter comes back through the door carrying what is left. We’re told, in one way or another, not to get too attached. But how do you see somebody almost every week for years, accept her cake, argue with her about whether you saved her life, and not get attached?

I keep thinking about that foil with my name on it.

Has anyone else had a patient like Mrs. H.? How do you carry those goodbyes, especially when the family comes back in and you have to find a way to be professional while your heart is breaking a little?
